Content:
An undirected graph is connected if there is a path between every pair of vertices. A graph is disconnected if at least two vertices have no path between them.

Content:
A component (or connected component) of an undirected graph is a connected subgraph that is not contained in any other connected subgraph.

Content:
From these definitions, we can prove the following:

- A connected graph consists of exactly one component.
- A disconnected graph consists of at least two components.
- An isolated vertex is a component.
- There is no path between vertices in different components.

A component (or connected component) of an undirected graph is a connected subgraph that is not contained in any other connected subgraph. Obviously, a single vertex with no edges is also a connected component.

Unlike undirected graphs, where connectivity is a single concept, directed graphs have three distinct types of connectivity: weakly connected, unilaterally connected, and strongly connected.

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
An undirected graph is connected if there is a path between every pair of vertices. A graph is disconnected if at least two vertices have no path between them.

Content:
A component (or connected component) of an undirected graph is a connected subgraph that is not contained in any other connected subgraph.

Content:
From these definitions, we can prove the following:

Content:
- A connected graph consists of exactly one component.
- A disconnected graph consists of at least two components.
- An isolated vertex is a component.
- There is no path between vertices in different components.

Content:
For example, consider the following graph:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/77cc4175b26a78e1e028538ea71fc0f6]

Content:
This graph has [MATH: 3] connected components, as shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/8d314fc83466e1a6a0d238c7cefa2c15]

---

Item 2 — Example: Identifying the Number of Connected Components in a Graph

Example Prompt:
[IMG: /graphics/a14fb6b1f43197f94dc740e90d09bd14]

How many connected components does the graph above have?

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
A component (or connected component) of an undirected graph is a connected subgraph that is not contained in any other connected subgraph. In a connected component, every pair of vertices is connected by a path, and no paths exist that lead to vertices outside the component. Obviously, a single vertex with no edges is also a connected component.

Our graph has [MATH: 2] connected components.

[IMG: /graphics/12cbfc20f90cec6568a497d405493dbc]

Item 5 — Tutorial: Weakly Connected Graphs

Content:
Unlike undirected graphs, where connectivity is a single concept, directed graphs have three distinct types of connectivity: weakly connected, unilaterally connected, and strongly connected.

Content:
A directed graph is weakly connected if replacing all directed edges with undirected edges results in a connected graph.

Content:
For example, consider the graph [MATH: G] below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/6ea962c9b1aefab986aee29973977ebf]

Content:
By replacing all directed edges with undirected ones, we obtain the following connected undirected graph:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/c83919ef868a2cdf1e01cf0cef19555f]

Content:
Therefore, the graph [MATH: G] is weakly connected.

| Edges: | [MATH: v_1 \to v_2,] [MATH: v_2 \to v_3,] [MATH: v_3 \to v_1,] [MATH: v_3 \to v_4] |

The vertices and edges of the directed graph [MATH: G] are given above. Determine whether the graph [MATH: G] is weakly connected or disconnected and how many weakly connected components it contains.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Recall that a component (or connected component) of an undirected graph is a connected subgraph that is not contained in any other connected subgraph. In a connected component, every pair of vertices is connected by a path, and no paths exist that lead to vertices outside the component. A single vertex with no edges is also a connected component.

A directed graph is weakly connected if the underlying undirected graph (i.e., the graph formed when the direction of the edges is removed) is connected.

First, let's sketch our directed graph.

[IMG: /graphics/7586082dc071aa6be743c28c56866dfc]

The corresponding undirected graph is shown below.

[IMG: /graphics/1b8622a28c5673b9b25cad9949936b80]

From the figure, we observe that the undirected graph is connected. So, our initial directed graph is weakly connected and has [MATH: 1] weakly connected component.

Item 9 — Tutorial: Strongly Connected and Unilaterally Connected Graphs

Content:
A directed graph is strongly connected if there is a directed path between every pair of vertices in both directions.

Content:
For example, consider the graph [MATH: G] below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/f7398e3e5512fe0645df408442ec23af]

Content:
In this graph, for every pair of vertices, there exists a directed path between them in both directions. For instance, for [MATH: v_1] and [MATH: v_2,] the paths [MATH: (v_1 \to v_2)] and [MATH: (v_2 \to v_3 \to v_1)] exist. Therefore, the graph [MATH: G] is strongly connected.

Content:
A directed graph is unilaterally connected (or semiconnected) if there is a directed path between each pair of vertices in at least one direction.

Content:
For example, consider the graph [MATH: G] below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/54fff6073a0fb3bfc61406e96b2ef7e3]

Content:
In this graph, for every pair of vertices, there exists a path in one direction: [MATH: (v_1 \to v_2), (v_2 \to v_3),] and [MATH: (v_1 \to v_2 \to v_3).] Therefore, the graph [MATH: G] is unilaterally connected. Note that it is not strongly connected, for example because there is no path from [MATH: v_2] to [MATH: v_1].
